metadata.title: Integrated Partnership Reasoning and Data Sufficiency
metadata.description: Choose and combine partnership methods, then decide whether statements provide enough information for a unique answer.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Integrate capital-time ratios, staged changes, unknown shares, and mixed agreements in fresh problems requiring a deliberate sequence of methods. For data sufficiency, test each statement alone, then both together; distinguish a unique numerical answer from a ratio-only result, identify redundant statements, and detect when information remains insufficient. Preserve the chapter’s answer-choice logic for two- and three-statement questions and justify every sufficiency conclusion algebraically. Ground in the chapter’s Data Sufficiency Questions 1–13 and mixed objective patterns.

content.text: Integrated Partnership Reasoning and Data Sufficiency: Choose and combine partnership methods, then decide whether statements provide enough information for a unique answer. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Integrated Partnership Reasoning and Data Sufficiency asks you to decide what determines each partner’s share. Choose and combine partnership methods, then decide whether statements provide enough information for a unique answer. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. Capstone problems require choosing the right partnership model, and data-sufficiency questions require testing uniqueness. Write the partner names and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

For sufficiency, test Statement I alone, Statement II alone, and both together. A statement is enough only if it fixes the requested value uniquely, not merely a ratio or one unknown relation. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once both are expressed in compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: If A:B:C=2:4:7 and Nitin’s share (7 parts) is known, Gagan’s 4-part share is fixed. The ratio alone without any total or one share cannot give a rupee amount. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Finish by checking both the numerical result and whether the supplied information really determines it. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. For each data condition, ask whether a free scale factor remains; use counterexamples to prove insufficiency. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: Do not assume an unstated investment duration or total profit. In capstones, write the needed timeline and profit pool before calculating. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. When multiple statement combinations work, report the exact sufficiency category rather than choosing the first plausible one. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for integrated partnership reasoning and data sufficiency without relying on a memorized answer pattern.

Ravi, Gagan, and Nitin share a partnership profit. Is Gagan’s amount known? I: Their investment ratio is 2:4:7. II: Nitin’s profit share is ₹8,750.

inlineData.prompt: Ravi, Gagan, and Nitin share a partnership profit. Is Gagan’s amount known? I: Their investment ratio is 2:4:7. II: Nitin’s profit share is ₹8,750.
hints: A ratio and a known partner share are both needed to establish a rupee amount.
Test each statement alone, then combine them.
inlineData.explanation: I gives only a ratio and no rupee scale. II gives one partner’s share but no relation to Gagan. Together, 7 parts=₹8,750, so Gagan receives 4/7×₹8,750=₹5,000.

A and B share annual profit ₹23,800. Find A’s share. I: B’s investment is 112.5% more than A’s. II: A invested ₹120,000.

inlineData.prompt: A and B share annual profit ₹23,800. Find A’s share. I: B’s investment is 112.5% more than A’s. II: A invested ₹120,000.
hints: A percent “more than” means the original 100% plus the stated increase.
Translate 112.5% more into 212.5% of A, then use the known profit total.
inlineData.explanation: If A=x, then B=(1+1.125)x=2.125x=17x/8, so A:B=8:17. A receives 8/25×₹23,800=₹7,616. II alone gives no B investment or ratio.

At the end of a two-year partnership, find Neeta’s share of ₹43,600 profit. I: Neeta invested ₹85,000. II: Seeta and Geeta joined after six months with capitals in ratio 3:5. III: Their combined capital was ₹250,000.

inlineData.prompt: At the end of a two-year partnership, find Neeta’s share of ₹43,600 profit. I: Neeta invested ₹85,000. II: Seeta and Geeta joined after six months with capitals in ratio 3:5. III: Their combined capital was ₹250,000.
hints: Without I Neeta’s weight is unknown; without II the two partners’ relative weights are unknown; without III their scale is unknown.
Use each statement to find one missing piece, then calculate all three capital-time weights.
inlineData.explanation: I supplies Neeta’s capital; II supplies the other partners’ ratio and 18-month duration; III sets their capital scale. Seeta=₹93,750 and Geeta=₹156,250. Weighted ratio=2,040,000:1,687,500:2,812,500=272:225:375. Neeta receives 272/872×₹43,600=₹13,600. Each statement is necessary.

Find the percentage share of Y in an equal-time partnership. I: X, Y, and Z invest for two years. II: Total profit equals 30% of total capital. III: Y invested as much as X and Z together.

inlineData.prompt: Find the percentage share of Y in an equal-time partnership. I: X, Y, and Z invest for two years. II: Total profit equals 30% of total capital. III: Y invested as much as X and Z together.
hints: A statement can determine a percentage share without giving any rupee amounts.
Use Y=X+Z to compare Y with the combined total.
inlineData.explanation: Statement III gives Y’s capital equal to X+Z, so Y has half the total capital. Equal durations make the profit ratio match capital, so Y receives 50%. I and II do not specify Y’s relative capital.

A and B start with capitals in ratio 3:5. After 4 months A increases capital by 50%; after 6 months B withdraws one-fifth of original capital. Year-end profit is ₹34,000. Find B’s share.

inlineData.prompt: A and B start with capitals in ratio 3:5. After 4 months A increases capital by 50%; after 6 months B withdraws one-fifth of original capital. Year-end profit is ₹34,000. Find B’s share.
hints: The stated increase applies to A’s original capital; B’s reduced amount applies only after month 6.
Build separate interval products, simplify 48:54 to 8:9, then allocate the total.
inlineData.explanation: Let starting capitals be 3x and 5x. A’s weight=3x×4+4.5x×8=48x. B’s weight=5x×6+4x×6=54x. Ratio=8:9, so B receives 9/17×₹34,000=₹18,000.

A and B start with capitals 4:6. After 3 months A increases capital by 50%; after 8 months B withdraws one-third of original capital. Year-end profit is ₹19,500. Find B’s share.

inlineData.prompt: A and B start with capitals 4:6. After 3 months A increases capital by 50%; after 8 months B withdraws one-third of original capital. Year-end profit is ₹19,500. Find B’s share.
hints: Do not apply either changed amount retroactively to the whole year.
Split the year at months 3 and 8 and add each partner’s weighted segments.
inlineData.explanation: A’s weight=4x×3+6x×9=66x. B’s weight=6x×8+4x×4=64x. Thus A:B=33:32 and B receives 32/65×₹19,500=₹9,600.
